confirmed.title: cli_api_ms is cumulative (sum of all sub-request times), not wall-clock — makes Health pane overhead formula wrong for agentic turns
confirmed.symptom: 13 of 42 turns (31%) show cli_api_ms > duration_ms, producing negative 'Rift overhead' in the AI Health pane. Worst case: opus+high turn with cli_api=503,576ms but wall-clock duration=105,118ms (ratio 4.8x). The Health pane formula 'overhead = duration_ms − cli_api_ms' yields −398,458ms for that turn.
confirmed.evidence: Telemetry: cli_api=503576ms dur=105118ms (4.8x); cli_api=399220ms dur=107932ms (3.7x); cli_api=35852ms dur=13292ms (2.7x). All 13 impossible turns are opus+high (6) or sonnet+medium (5) or opus+medium (2). p50 non_api_overhead across all 42 turns = 971ms but if negatives excluded = 1514ms. The CLI's duration_api_ms field is documented as 'total wall-time spent in API calls' but for agentic multi-tool turns it is the sum of individual request durations (e.g. 5 sequential 100s requests = 500s accumulated vs 105s real wall-clock). perf.rs:83-87 comment and turn.rs:2542-2548 log both treat it as wall-clock.
confirmed.fix: Guard the overhead computation: when cli_api_ms > duration_ms, log a warning and exclude that turn from p50_non_api_overhead aggregation (or clamp overhead to 0). Add a note in the Health pane tooltip that cli_api_ms is cumulative for agentic turns. The attribution formula 'Rift overhead = duration − cli_api' is only valid for single-request turns.

reasons: Fully confirmed by both telemetry and source. Telemetry shows 13/42 turns (31%) where cli_api_ms exceeds duration_ms by ratios up to 4.8x (503,576ms vs 105,118ms wall-clock). perf.rs:349-350 uses `saturating_sub` which clamps these to 0 rather than excluding them, silently polluting the p50_non_api_overhead_ms median with zeros. The source comment at perf.rs:308-309 mischaracterizes this as minor "tool-work overlap" when the actual ratios prove it's cumulative multi-request accumulation from agentic turns. The Health pane's attribution formula (overhead = duration − cli_api) is documented as wall-clock separation at perf.rs:83-87 and turn.rs:2488-2489/2543-2548, but cli_api_ms is the sum of sequential per-request durations for agentic turns. The p50 computed from 13 clamped-zero turns mixed with 29 valid turns misrepresents Rift's true overhead. Evidence is real; this is a genuine data-quality bug in the metric aggregation and its framing in the Health pane.

The root phenomenon is confirmed: 13/42 turns (31%) show cli_api_ms > duration_ms with the exact ratios the claim cites (worst: 4.79×, cli_api=503,576ms vs dur=105,118ms for opus+high). The CLI's duration_api_ms field is indeed cumulative for agentic multi-tool turns, not wall-clock.

However, the claim is partially wrong about the symptom: the Health pane never shows negative overhead. perf.rs:350 uses `dur.saturating_sub(api)` which clamps every impossible turn to 0. The comment at line 305-309 even acknowledges the pattern ("a turn whose tool work overlaps API streaming can read slightly negative — that's not 'negative overhead'"). No negative number reaches the UI.

The actual (real but subtler) bug is that clamping to 0 — instead of excluding — skews the p50 downward. With the 13 zero-clamped turns included, p50_non_api_overhead_ms = 944ms. Excluding impossible turns gives 1514ms (exactly matching the claim's stated exclusion figure). So the UI's "Rift overhead" figure is underestimated by ~38%. The avg_cli_api_ms of 57,990ms is also inflated by the agentic turns' accumulated sub-request times, making the "98% is Claude thinking" split somewhat misleading — though directionally correct.

The fix described (exclude rather than clamp impossible turns from the p50 aggregation, and add a tooltip noting cli_api_ms is cumulative for agentic turns) is warranted. The log warning in turn.rs:2548-2552 already shows negative overhead in the log for these turns; the backend just silently swallows it with saturating_sub rather than flagging it as a data-quality issue. Severity T2 is appropriate — real data accuracy issue with meaningful user-visible effect (overhead p50 off by 38%), but no crash, no security issue, and the UI direction is correct.

confirmed.title: Haiku turns run with full default CLI thinking despite effort=low because --effort flag AND thinking-disable shim are both intentionally skipped for haiku
confirmed.symptom: All 4 haiku turns (effort=low in FE telemetry) have ttft_thinking_ms present (3193, 8175, 8296, 8678ms). Resulting ttft_text_ms is 8042–20966ms — significantly slower than the sonnet p50 of 4431ms. Haiku is chosen for 'quick' tasks but behaves like a full-thinking model.
confirmed.evidence: turn.rs:1104: `else if !thinking_on && model != "haiku"` — thinking-disable shim is NOT applied for haiku. turn.rs:1177: `if !cfg.local_llm_enabled && model != "haiku" && caps.effort` — --effort flag is NOT sent for haiku. Result: haiku runs with the CLI's own default effort (which includes extended thinking). Telemetry confirms: haiku thinking=[3193, 8175, 8296, 8678]ms, dominant_cause='thinking' on 3 of 4 turns. Haiku median ttft_text=17448ms vs sonnet p50=4431ms.
confirmed.fix: The code comments say 'Haiku has no extended thinking' (turn.rs:1107) and 'API rejects effort on Haiku 4.5' (turn.rs:1116), but telemetry shows thinking IS occurring. Investigate whether Haiku 4.5 now accepts --effort or the thinking observed comes from the CLI's default pre-pass. If the API now supports it, apply --effort low for haiku when thinking_on=false (remove the model != "haiku" guard from line 1177). Note: haiku guard at line 668 already falls back to sonnet post-2026-06-26, so this only affects historical turns and any re-enabled haiku path.

reasons: Evidence confirmed. All 4 haiku turns (2026-06-25) ran with `ttft_thinking_ms` present [3193, 8175, 8296, 8678ms], and the code at turn.rs:1104 and :1177 does intentionally skip both the nothink shim and the `--effort` flag when `model == "haiku"`. The comment rationale ("Haiku has no extended thinking", "API rejects effort on Haiku 4.5") is falsified by the telemetry — the CLI's own default effort (`high`) produced full thinking on haiku 4.5 turns, causing median ttft_text ~17s vs sonnet p50 ~4.4s. However, the bug is now historical-only: `HAIKU_DISABLED = true` (config.rs:245) makes `haiku_unavailable()` always return true, so line 668 already redirects any haiku turn to sonnet before reaching the effort/shim guards. Lines 1104/1177's `model != "haiku"` guards are dead code in current production. The proposed fix (removing the haiku guard from line 1177) is logically correct but has zero production impact since haiku can never reach it. Severity is appropriate as a documented-but-now-moot design flaw.

Claim is real and accurately described. The fix (remove the `model != "haiku"` guard from line 1177 so `--effort low` is sent for haiku) is correct but affects only a re-enable scenario. confirmed.title: Opus first-line arrives in <300ms but text takes up to 55s: 12 turns with 10–53s silent gap between stream start and first text token
confirmed.symptom: 12 Opus turns show ttft_first_line_ms < 500ms (stream starts fast) but ttft_text_ms > 10,000ms — the model is silent between streaming start and first text for 10–53 seconds. This gap is the unacknowledged 'thinking silence' that the user experiences as a hang.
confirmed.evidence: Worst 5 gaps: [first=131ms, text=53118ms, gap=52987ms, effort=high]; [first=139ms, text=40539ms, gap=40400ms, effort=high]; [first=156ms, text=31127ms, gap=30971ms, effort=high]; [first=157ms, text=29241ms, gap=29084ms, effort=medium]; [first=0ms, text=14195ms, gap=14195ms, effort=medium]. All 12 are opus; 7 are effort=high. ttft_thinking_ms confirms thinking is active on 11 of 12. But thinking_ms (2164–7534ms) does not account for the full gap — e.g. gap=52987ms with thinking=3186ms means 50s of unaccounted streaming silence after thinking tokens finish.
confirmed.fix: The gap between ttft_thinking_ms and ttft_text_ms (post-thinking silence before first text token) is the tool-output processing phase. Consider streaming a 'thinking complete, generating response...' indicator once thinking tokens end, keyed off the ttft_thinking_ms event. This would eliminate the perceived hang without changing the underlying model behavior.

reasons:
Core evidence is real and verified exactly: 12 Opus turns with first_line_ms < 500ms and ttft_text_ms > 10s, worst 5 numbers match to the millisecond, post-thinking silences range from 6.6s to 49.9s. dominant_cause='thinking' on 10/12.

Two nuances from re-verification:

1. Mechanism hypothesis is wrong: The claim attributes the post-thinking silence to "tool-output processing," but pre_text_tool_ms is NULL for 11/12 of these turns. There are no tool calls happening in that gap — it's pure model generation latency after thinking tokens finish (the model composing its response). This doesn't affect severity but makes the claim's mechanical explanation incorrect.

2. Proposed fix is partially already implemented: StreamTurn.svelte already detects when thinking ends (endThinking() sets status='done', activeThinkingIndex=null) and immediately transitions to "Working…" + animated whim-word cycling ("Sussing…", "Spelunking…", "Pondering…" every 2.4s). The stallLevel watchdog also shows escalating copy at 20s/60s/150s. The post-thinking gap is NOT a completely silent hang — it has animated busy-state feedback. The claim overstates severity by calling it "the unacknowledged thinking silence."

Bottom line: the data pattern is confirmed real and worth attention. A more specific "Generating response…" label after thinking completes (vs. the generic whim words) could reduce user confusion, but it's a UX polish item, not fixing a silent hang. Severity T2 is a slight overstatement given existing animation, but defensible for the 30–50s extreme cases where even animated cycling reads as a hang.

The claim misreads the telemetry schema. `ttft_thinking_ms` is time-from-turn-start to the FIRST thinking token (confirmed in turn.rs:2331 — set when `is_think && !first_think_logged`), NOT the duration of thinking. The "post-thinking silence" the claim computes as `gap - thinking_ms` is actually `ttft_text_ms - ttft_thinking_ms`, which is the complete thinking duration (entirely expected — the model is actively streaming thinking tokens during this interval). There is no unaccounted silence. The 10–53s gaps are simply how long extended Opus thinking takes; they're dominated by the thinking phase completing, not a pipeline stall after it ends. The proposed fix is also broken: it would key a "thinking complete" indicator off `ttft_thinking_ms`, which fires at thinking START, not end.

The symptom is real and confirmed. All 9 claude-fable-5 turns have ttft_text_ms=null, ttft_thinking_ms=null, and cli_api_ms=null despite result_subtype=success. confirmed.title: Dominant premature eviction cause: effort_level baked into SpawnKey triggers cold respawn on every effort-tier change
confirmed.symptom: 15/19 premature evictions are warm-child drain + cold respawn (TTFT jumps from ~100-200ms warm to ~1500ms cold) triggered when effort_level or thinking_on changes between consecutive turns in the same session.
confirmed.evidence: Log lines confirm mechanism: '2026-06-25T16:42:35.112Z warm_pool: signature changed for 8821361a — draining + cold respawn' (logged 10+ times in session 8821361a). Each is immediately preceded by 'assistant_send: session 8821361a pinned to model sonnet (picker=opus) — preserving thinking-block signatures'. The SpawnKey struct at turn.rs:1291-1303 includes effort_level (line 1300) and thinking_on (line 1299); mismatch check at turn.rs:1361 triggers the drain. Session 8821361a has 13 premature evictions from rapid effort cycling (low->medium->high at 0.5-0.7s intervals — sub-human, dev test session). Real-user sessions: 1054b011 (high->medium, gap 14.2s), 320337a3 (high->low, gap 9.3s, 'drained + reaped old child pid=65104'), a3c72b60 (low->high, gap 45.7s, 'drained + reaped old child pid=33576').
confirmed.fix: warm_pool.rs constants (MAX_WARM=20, IDLE_EVICT=7200s, IDLE_EVICT_PRESSURE=1800s) cannot fix this — they control idle eviction only, not SpawnKey mismatch. --effort is baked into CLI argv and cannot be hot-swapped. Actionable options: (A) Multi-child pool keyed by (session_id, effort_level) so a session keeps up to 3 warm children at different effort levels — eliminates the respawn when user cycles effort mid-session, cost ~3x RAM per active session. (B) Reduce FE effort volatility: once a user sends the first turn, lock the effort picker for that session until reset (would have prevented all 13 dev-test evictions and the 3 real-user ones). (C) Accept current behavior — only 3 real-user premature evictions from this cause (session 8821361a is automated testing); the respawn cost (~1.4s TTFT delta) is a one-time penalty per effort change.

reasons: All core evidence verified. Log evidence: session `8821361a` has exactly 13 signature-changed events (verified in log), all preceded by "pinned to model sonnet" lines. Each cold respawn shows TTFT 1465-1526ms vs 7-185ms warm. The three named real-user sessions (`1054b011`: high→medium, 14.15s gap; `320337a3`: high→low, 8.86s result-to-next; `a3c72b60`: low→high, 45.6s result-to-next) all match the claimed gaps and all show "drained + reaped old child pid=..." as stated. Fix analysis is accurate: idle eviction constants (MAX_WARM, IDLE_EVICT) are irrelevant to SpawnKey mismatch — they only gate the idle-eviction path, not the key-mismatch drain path. Minor inaccuracy in claim: the "3 real-user premature evictions" figure is an undercount — at least 4 mid-session effort-cycling events appear in the current log (also `87a27f20`), plus ~11 additional sessions where prewarm key mismatches the actual first turn (model change between prewarm and real turn — a related but distinct failure mode not named in the claim). None of these undermine the claim; they strengthen it. T2 severity is appropriate: real, reproducible, affects user-visible TTFT but only on effort-tier changes, and the worst session (`8821361a`) was dev testing. The fix options described are accurate: multi-child pool keyed by (session,effort), FE effort stabilization, or accept it. Not safe to autofix — Option B (lock effort post-first-turn) requires FE state machine changes with product tradeoffs, Option A requires significant warm_pool restructuring.

Mechanism is real and source-confirmed. SpawnKey at turn.rs:1291-1303 includes effort_level (line 1300) and thinking_on (line 1299); mismatch at line 1361 triggers drain + cold respawn. Source comment at lines 116-118 explicitly marks this as intentional design: "effort change MUST respawn. Silent wrong-effort is worse than a cold turn." The behavior is explicitly documented as intentional in source code and is working as designed. T2 is too high given only 3 real-user instances and explicit intentional design rationale; the actual actionable issue (prewarm→first-turn thinking_on mismatch as a separate pattern) is unaccounted for in the claim's framing.

confirmed.title: bg-spawn forced eviction: run_in_background Bash turns deliberately evict warm child (M3 pipe-taint protection)
confirmed.symptom: 2/19 premature evictions in session b86a6a85 (gaps 94.8s and 106.1s, both medium->medium same effort) are intentional forced evictions after turns that spawn background Bash children.
confirmed.evidence: Log lines: '2026-06-25T20:46:53 warm_pool: run_in_background Bash detected — will evict warm child after turn, session=b86a6a85' and '2026-06-25T20:47:44 warm_pool: bg-spawn turn — evicting warm child b86a6a85'. Same pattern repeats at 20:51:27 and 20:52:13. Telemetry shows was_cold=True on the NEXT turns (turns 4 and 5, gaps 94.8s and 106.1s from previous turn end). This is M3 protection: a background child inherits the warm stdin write-end, preventing the pipe from ever EOF-ing, which would strand the warm child.
confirmed.fix: This is working as designed (M3 correctness requirement documented in warm_pool.rs:30-35). No warm_pool.rs constant change can help — the eviction is triggered by the background spawn, not idle time. If this TTFT cost is unacceptable, the fix would require the CLI to support a way to detach background children from the parent's stdio, which is a Claude CLI upstream change. Current behavior is correct.

The M3 mechanism is fully implemented and the cited log lines exist verbatim in source. turn.rs:2288-2293 detects `run_in_background: true` Bash tool_use and sets `bg_evict`; turn.rs:1904-1906 reads that flag after the turn's `result` frame and breaks the warm-reuse loop, emitting exactly the log lines the claim cites. warm_pool.rs:31-32 documents this as an intentional correctness requirement (background child inherits stdout write-end → pipe never EOFs → warm child stranded). confirmed.title: Dead-pipe eviction: warm child self-exits while parked, next turn gets cold retry
confirmed.symptom: 2/19 premature evictions are dead-pipe: the warm child exited on its own while idle and the next turn found it dead, triggering a cold retry.
confirmed.evidence: Log lines: '2026-06-25T21:02:58 warm_pool: reused turn found dead child b86a6a85 — signalling cold retry' (session b86a6a85, after a prior bg-eviction window race) and '2026-06-25T23:00:12 warm_pool: reused turn found dead child 4aa5c7f5 — signalling cold retry' (session 4aa5c7f5, gap 54.9s, same effort medium->medium). Also '2026-06-28T09:56:15 warm_pool: pre-warm spare a3c72b60 died while parked — silent cold retry' (pre-warm spare death, not a turn-to-turn eviction). The child self-exits without an explicit eviction trigger.
confirmed.fix: warm_pool.rs constants cannot prevent the child from self-exiting (e.g., Claude CLI internal timeout or OOM). The cold retry path already handles it gracefully (--resume preserves context). To reduce frequency: investigate whether the CLI exits cleanly under specific conditions (empty result, error subtype) that could be caught and the child pre-replaced. confirmed.title: opener:allow-open-url blocks http:// links — AI-generated non-https URLs silently fail to open
confirmed.symptom: Clicking any http:// link in AI-generated chat output does nothing; no browser opens, no error shown to user.
confirmed.evidence: default.json allow list: [{"url": "https://**"}, {"url": "mailto:*"}] — no http://**. Markdown.svelte:332: `const safe = /^https?:\/\//i.test(href) || href.startsWith("mailto:");` — passes both http and https. Markdown.svelte:341: `void openUrl(href).catch((err) => console.warn("openUrl failed", err))` — blocked call is swallowed as console.warn. contextMenu.svelte.ts:196: `if (link?.href && /^https?:/i.test(link.href))` then line 203: `await openUrl(link.href)` — same mismatch. Tauri capability layer rejects the IPC call; JS catches it silently.
confirmed.fix: Either (a) add `{ "url": "http://**" }` to the allow list in both default.json and secondary-window.json to permit http:// external opens, or (b) tighten both regexes to `^https:\/\/` only and drop http:// support — the latter is the safer choice given the assistant deals in current web content which is overwhelmingly https.

reasons:
Evidence is real. Both capability files confirmed: `opener:allow-open-url` allows only `https://**` + `mailto:*` — no `http://**`. Markdown.svelte:332 regex `^https?:\/\/` passes http:// links to `openUrl()`. contextMenu.svelte.ts:196 same mismatch. The silent-swallow at line 341 (`console.warn`) is confirmed.

However, the http:// exclusion is INTENTIONAL — commit 300b6e0 (2026-06-15) explicitly removed it as a security hardening: "capabilities: drop http://** from opener:allow-open-url (https-only)". This is documented deliberate policy, not an oversight.

The actual bug is the JS-side regex being inconsistent with that intentional policy: the frontend still treats http:// as "safe" and routes it to `openUrl()`, which silently fails due to the capability block. The fix should be option (b) from the claim — tighten both regexes to `^https:\/\/` (drop the `?`) to align with the established https-only policy. This is a real but narrow UX inconsistency: http:// links appear clickable but do nothing, with no user feedback. T3 is generous; T2 (cosmetic/minor UX gap) is more accurate since there's no data loss, security hole, or functional regression — the capability block is working as designed.

The https-only allow list in both capability files is intentional and already tracked. ISSUES.md:312 explicitly records: "capabilities/default.json opener:allow-open-url — dropped http://***, https-only (this session)" as a completed security fix. The JS regex still accepting http:// (Markdown.svelte:332, contextMenu.svelte.ts:196) while the capability blocks it is a real inconsistency, but it's a known post-fix residual state, not an unreported bug. The claim presents an already-resolved, intentional security decision as an untracked silent failure.

killed.title: reqwest 'rustls' feature activates aws-lc-rs as default crypto provider (silent provider conflict risk)
killed.why: The claimed panic scenario does not occur in practice. Both reqwest 0.13.3 and ureq 3.3.0 (velopack's HTTP client) bypass `rustls::crypto::CryptoProvider::get_default_or_install_from_crate_features()` entirely — the function that panics when both providers are compiled in. Instead they each call the safe `CryptoProvider::get_default()` and fall back to their own provider: reqwest falls back to `aws_lc_rs::default_provider()` (via its `default_rustls_crypto_provider()` at reqwest/src/async_impl/client.rs:2459-2464), ureq falls back to `ring::default_provider()` (via `ring_if_enabled()` at ureq/src/tls/rustls.rs:148-150). Both use `ClientConfig::builder_with_provider()`, not `ClientConfig::builder()`. So the "second install_default panics" theory is moot — neither library installs a default at all. The two providers coexist in the binary without conflict; reqwest TLS uses aws-lc-rs and ureq/velopack TLS uses ring, but this is not a race or panic risk — it's just two independent provider instances. The subsidiary claim that the direct `rustls = { features = ["ring"] }` dep drops aws-lc-rs from the tree is also wrong (cargo tree confirms aws-lc-rs remains; reqwest's `rustls` feature hardcodes `__rustls-aws-lc-rs`), but that inaccuracy doesn't produce the alleged runtime failure. No panic observed, no install_default conflict, behavior is deterministic not implementation-defined.
